match.reason: No bank point teaches the spectrum of market structures from perfect competition to monopoly or how market power affects prices and efficiency; the closest, competition policy, covers the law against anti-competitive conduct, not the market structures themselves.

draft.title: Market structures
card: Market structures sort markets by how much power sellers have over price. Market power is a firm's ability to influence the price it charges.
Perfect competition
many small sellers of identical products, so no firm has any power over price.
Monopolistic competition
many sellers of similar but differentiated products, such as cafés. Each firm has a little market power.
Oligopoly and monopoly
an oligopoly has a few large firms that dominate the market. A monopoly has one seller and the most market power.
draft.remember: More market power usually means higher prices and less efficient use of resources.

a.q: Which market structure has a few large firms that dominate the market?
opts: Oligopoly
Monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Perfect competition
a.why: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms. A monopoly is tempting, but it has only one seller, not a few.
a.clue: Count the sellers: not one, and not many.

b.q: Only one company supplies water to a remote town in Victoria, and there are no rivals. Compared with a market with many sellers, what is most likely?
opts: Higher prices and less efficient use of resources
Lower prices and more efficient use of resources
Higher prices and more efficient use of resources
Lower prices and less efficient use of resources
b.why: One seller with no rivals is a monopoly, which has the most market power. More market power usually means higher prices and less efficient use of resources. Lower prices are wrong because a firm with power over price has less reason to cut them.
b.clue: Think about how much power the only seller has over price.

b.best: Higher prices and less efficient use of resources

problems.detail: Water supply to a remote town is a classic natural monopoly. One supplier can be cheaper than many rival networks, and in Victoria water is supplied by government-owned corporations whose prices are regulated by the Essential Services Commission. So 'higher prices' is not clearly the likely outcome here. A non-regulated example, such as the only petrol station or shop in a remote town, would test the idea without this clash.

check.summary: The card and question a are sound. Question b uses Victorian town water as its monopoly example, but that is a regulated natural monopoly where higher prices and less efficiency are not clearly the likely result, so a different single-seller example would be safer.

b.q: Kai runs the only petrol station in a remote town, and the nearest rival is hours away. Compared with many sellers, what is most likely?
opts: Higher prices and less efficient use of resources
Lower prices and more efficient use of resources
Higher prices and more efficient use of resources
Lower prices and less efficient use of resources
